title: One-to-many
summary: Navigation properties, foreign keys, and how EF Core links rows when you link objects.

steps.title: Authors and books
body: An author writes many books; each book has one author. In the database that is a **foreign key**: a column in `Books` holding the id of a row in `Authors`.
In C# you describe it with **navigation properties**, references between objects:
```csharp
class Author
public int Id { get; set; }
public string Name { get; set; } = "";
public List<Book> Books { get; set; } = [];     // collection navigation
class Book
public int Id { get; set; }
public string Title { get; set; } = "";
public int AuthorId { get; set; }                // foreign key property
public Author Author { get; set; } = null!;      // reference navigation

EF Core pairs `Author.Books` with `Book.Author` and recognises `AuthorId` as the foreign key by its name (navigation name + `Id`). The `Books` table gets an `AuthorId INTEGER NOT NULL` column, an index on it, and `REFERENCES "Authors" ("Id")`.
`= null!` on `Author` says: "this is never null once loaded, but EF Core fills it in, not my constructor".

steps.prompt: Match each part of the relationship to its name.
steps.explain: The **principal** (Author) is the one being pointed at; the **dependent** (Book) holds the foreign key. A book cannot exist without its author, so the dependent is the side that depends.

steps.title: Linking objects links rows
body: You almost never set `AuthorId` by hand. Link the objects and EF Core fills in the keys when it saves:
```csharp fragment
var leGuin = new Author { Name = "Le Guin" };
leGuin.Books.Add(new Book { Title = "Earthsea" });
db.Books.Add(new Book { Title = "The Dispossessed", Author = leGuin });
db.Authors.Add(leGuin);
db.SaveChanges();

One `SaveChanges` inserts the author first (it needs its id), then both books with `AuthorId` set to it. Adding the author also added the books reachable from it: EF Core follows navigations when you `Add`.
If you already know an author's id, setting the foreign key is fine too, and saves a query: `new Book { Title = "Dune", AuthorId = 2 }`.

code: var dune = new Book { Title = "Dune", Author = herbert };
public Author Author { get; set; } = null!;
protected override void OnConfiguring(DbContextOptionsBuilder options) => options.UseSqlite("Data Source=library.db");
steps.explain: Before saving, the foreign key is still 0: the author has no id yet. Saving inserts Herbert (id 1), then the book with `AuthorId = 1`. EF Core also **fixes up** the other side: `herbert.Books` now contains `dune`, although your code never added it there.

steps.prompt: A `Book` has `int AuthorId` (not `int?`). What does that say about the relationship?
options: Every book must have an author: the relationship is required
A book may have no author
An author can have only one book
The author is deleted when the book is
steps.explain: A non-nullable foreign key makes the relationship **required**: the column is `NOT NULL`. Make it `int?` (and the navigation `Author?`) for an optional relationship. That choice also decides what happens on delete (lesson 4).

steps.prompt: Complete the dependent side of an order-to-lines relationship.
steps.explain: The foreign key is named after the navigation plus `Id`, the reference navigation points at the principal, and the principal's collection holds dependents.

code: seed.Authors.Add(new Author { Name = "Le Guin", Books = [new() { Title = "Earthsea" }, new() { Title = "The Dispossessed" }] });
public Author Author { get; set; } = null!;
protected override void OnConfiguring(DbContextOptionsBuilder options) => options.UseSqlite("Data Source=library.db");
steps.explain: A query loads only what you ask for. `db.Books` reads book rows, so the foreign key `AuthorId` is there but the `Author` navigation is still `null`: nobody loaded the author. Lesson 3 shows how to load related data.
hints: Did the query mention authors at all?

steps.prompt: Which side holds the foreign key?
items: A book has one author, an author many books
An author has one portrait, and you put `PortraitId` on `Author`
A book has many tags, a tag many books
A book has one publisher, a publisher many books
steps.explain: In one-to-many the "many" side holds the key. In one-to-one you choose (here the author points at its portrait). Many-to-many needs a third table holding pairs of keys.

steps.title: Teams and players
prompt: Then write `int AddTeam(LeagueDb db, string name, params string[] players)` (at the top) that creates a team with those players numbered 1, 2, 3... in order, saves everything with **one** `SaveChanges`, and returns the team's id.
starter: int AddTeam(LeagueDb db, string name, params string[] players)
solution: int AddTeam(LeagueDb db, string name, params string[] players)
var team = new Team { Name = name };
team.Players.Add(new Player { Name = players[i], Number = i + 1 });
public Team Team { get; set; } = null!;
protected override void OnConfiguring(DbContextOptionsBuilder options) => options.UseSqlite("Data Source=league.db");
template: Dojo.Check("Players.TeamId is a required foreign key", dojoSql.Contains("\"TeamId\" INTEGER NOT NULL") && dojoSql.Contains("REFERENCES \"Teams\" (\"Id\")"), dojoSql);
Dojo.Eq("returns the team ids", new List<int> { 1, 2 }, new List<int> { dojoA, dojoB });
var dojoLions = dojoDb.Players.Where(p => p.TeamId == 1).OrderBy(p => p.Number).Select(p => p.Number + " " + p.Name).ToList();
Dojo.Eq("the Lions are numbered in order", new List<string> { "1 Ana", "2 Ben", "3 Cy" }, dojoLions);
Dojo.Eq("Dee plays for the Owls", "Owls", dojoDb.Players.Where(p => p.Name == "Dee").Select(p => p.Team.Name).Single());
hints: Add the players to `team.Players`, then add the team: EF Core inserts everything reachable from it.
